name: Ross syndrome
aliases: tonic pupil with areflexia and segmental anhidrosis

reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / Low's Clinical Autonomic Disorders
clinicalPearls: Classic triad of a tonic (Adie) pupil, generalised areflexia (absent deep tendon reflexes), and segmental anhidrosis
Patients often present with areas of absent sweating alongside compensatory hyperhidrosis in the intact skin, which is the usual presenting complaint
Regarded as a progressive disorder of the peripheral autonomic (cholinergic) neurons
Overlaps with Holmes-Adie syndrome (tonic pupil plus areflexia) and Harlequin syndrome, forming a spectrum of partial dysautonomia
Heat intolerance results from the reduced sweating surface area
The tonic pupil is large, poorly reactive to light, constricts slowly (tonically) to near effort, and shows cholinergic denervation supersensitivity to dilute pilocarpine
Diagnosis is clinical, supported by sweat testing to map the anhidrotic segments
Management is symptomatic: avoid heat, manage troublesome compensatory hyperhidrosis, and reassure
reference.pathophysiology: Ross syndrome is a progressive partial dysautonomia characterised by degeneration of postganglionic cholinergic autonomic neurons. Loss of sudomotor fibres produces patchy, segmental anhidrosis, while adjacent intact regions sweat excessively (compensatory hyperhidrosis) in an attempt to maintain thermoregulation. Involvement of the ciliary ganglion produces a tonic pupil with cholinergic denervation supersensitivity, and degeneration of dorsal root ganglion cells or their fibres underlies the generalised areflexia. The condition is thought to be a chronic, possibly immune-mediated or degenerative neuropathy of the peripheral autonomic and sensory systems, and it overlaps clinically with Holmes-Adie syndrome.
additionalInvestigations: Thermoregulatory sweat test to delineate anhidrotic and hyperhidrotic segments
Dilute pilocarpine pupil testing for cholinergic supersensitivity
Deep tendon reflex examination and, where needed, nerve conduction studies
Screening for associated autoimmune disease such as Sjogren syndrome
Skin biopsy for sudomotor nerve fibre assessment where available
redFlags: Rapidly progressive anhidrosis with heat intolerance risking hyperthermia
Features suggesting a wider or central autonomic disorder
Systemic symptoms suggesting an underlying autoimmune or paraneoplastic process
reference.prognosis: Ross syndrome tends to progress slowly, with the area of anhidrosis gradually enlarging over years; it is not life-threatening, but heat intolerance and troublesome compensatory hyperhidrosis can impair quality of life.
pitfalls: Focusing on the hyperhidrosis and missing the underlying anhidrosis and autonomic diagnosis
Failing to recognise the tonic pupil and areflexia that complete the triad
Attempting to suppress compensatory sweating, which may worsen heat intolerance
Not distinguishing it from Holmes-Adie syndrome and the wider dysautonomia spectrum
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Symptomatic control of compensatory hyperhidrosis with topical antiperspirants, anticholinergic agents or botulinum toxin injection
Advice on heat-avoidance and active cooling strategies to manage impaired thermoregulation from the reduced sweating surface
Dilute pilocarpine drops for symptomatic photophobia or near-vision difficulty from the tonic pupil
Reassurance regarding the benign, slowly progressive and non-life-threatening course
Screening for associated autoimmune disease such as Sjogren syndrome
Neurology and autonomic specialist referral for characterisation and long-term follow-up
